title: Refactoring Game help
author: Equivalent-Bell-6961
selftext: Hey, I am looking to refactor my game into smaller, modular pieces. Can someone give me some good industry practices to do this smoothly, using codex? It's not a very big game.

comments.author: tastygnar
comments.body: Start by asking the agent to evaluate the code against your ideal architecture, then put it to work

comments.author: Former_Produce1721
comments.body:
What kind of game is it?

There are many different architectural approaches in game dev that depend on the type of game and size of game you are making

Also what is it built in? That will also greatly affect it.

replies.author: Equivalent-Bell-6961
replies.body: Hey. It's a simple math game. I built it using codex - it is written in typescript.

comments.author: LatentBlade
comments.body: This is a hard question. You can always refactor more and there is a point of diminishing returns. Why do you think you need to refactor in the first place? I've never tried this with codex but generally you want to break functions into single a purpose. Taking an existing function and breaking it into parts is easier than generating it and it's a good way to understand your code better.

replies.author: Equivalent-Bell-6961
replies.body:
I'm a pure vibecoder. Learning-by-doing.

I made the base game, and it was basically an excel sheet. Then, I spent time with LLMs restructuring it out into a fully fleshed out game. Set up the whole plan, asked codex to make it - it did.

But it basically put all the game logic in one file, and the design logic in another.

I forgot/didn't know (blend of both) to ask it to make it modular from scratch when it was making the entire transformation - so I'm doing it now.

It's still small and coherent enough for it to be done safely, I hope.

Asking for good industry practices from those that know better than me, so that I can minimise chances of messing up.

replies.author: LatentBlade
replies.body: If you aren't planning on looking at the code why are you refactoring? The industry standard is to refactor for maintainability or efficiency

replies.author: LatentBlade
replies.body: I guess it depends how big the files are. Are you worried about context windows?

replies.author: Equivalent-Bell-6961
replies.body:
That's a bad assumption. I'm learning-by-doing, we're not all idiots lol. I do read what it codes, I do go through the source code, I have it explain stuff to me, I'm trying to understand bit by bit as I build.

and yeah - I want to refactor it for maintainability and efficiency, and to smoothen out the routing and nav so that it's easier to build future components.

I'm mainly worried about, like you'd expect, not knowing how to spot if it has missed something critical in a refactor. I also really believe in prevention being better than cure, and I'm humble enough to admit I'm not a coder at all, and basically clueless. So if someone has done big refactors before, gleaning knowledge or access to some tools could smoothen it out for me.

If you're interested, I did it successfully using this prompt-  
"Proceed with structuring out the refactoring plan. Uee this skill stack and construct the plan for in-line refactoring:  
  
Updated Inline Refactor Skill Stack  
  
superpowers:brainstorming  
Define the refactor design before coding.  
  
superpowers:writing-plans  
Convert the approved design into a concrete inline execution plan.  
  
refactoring-patterns  
Primary implementation skill for behavior-preserving extractions.  
  
clean-architecture  
Keep boundaries clean: shared domain, server adapters, client features.  
  
test-strategy  
Decide what tests protect each slice.  
  
jest-vitest  
Add or adjust unit tests where needed.  
  
frontend-developer  
Use when extracting React screens/components/hooks.  
  
absolute-ui  
Use only when visible UI/styling is touched.  
  
clean-code  
Cleanup pass after extraction.  
  
systematic-debugging  
Use when a regression appears.  
  
verification-before-completion  
Required before calling each slice done."

Feel free to roast me, or be kind and tell me if I did something badly. Idc, I'll take either approach - either way I will learn.

replies.author: LatentBlade
replies.body: Sorry. I didn't mean to imply that. I'm trying to understand pure vibe coding and it's difficult for me.

replies.author: LatentBlade
replies.body: I was going to suggest testing and are you have that in your prompt. Pay attention to what tests it writes. They will make sure you don't break things as you go and also will be a good test of how modular this is. I don't believe you mentioned react before. I don't know as much about that but I've written a lot of angular.  In general, I try to keep my components (UI elements) separate from my services (logic layer) and keep my components very small. I think you should try to define what your components should be and ask to break them down. Apologies if something I say doesn't make sense for react

comments.author: Kindly_Life_947
comments.body:
Divide code in to folders. fe. Plugins/module... The for each plugin asmdef.   
This avoid circular dependencies and makes the compilation faster because only the modules that change recompile on script change. The have a base code that uses these modules fe. game basecode. Use good old mvc or similar pattern. If this is not possible ask codex to do it. Now enjoy good coding and don't forget the tests

comments.body: set to 5.5 high/xhigh Ask codex to review the architecture, seeking out areas to decouple monoliths into deep modules (I recommend this wording specifically otherwise bro will fragment a 5000 loc file into 35 tiny modules). then just let him rip

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body:
Just because you use AI doesn't mean you can't learn to code. There are multiple answers and the right one will come to you if you understand coding.

For example, if your game contains multiple enemies, you want an Enemy class. If it contains collectible items you want an Item class. Probably you need a GameManager as well. If that one gets too big, split it up further into a LevelManager, UIManager, AssetManagers etc
